questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank:
Young players ________ the captain because of his hard work and fairness.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) look up to
Why: "Look up to" means to admire and respect someone.
Why not the others: (A) means to watch for. (B) means to regard as inferior. (C) means to pay a short visit.
Key point: Look up to (admire) is the opposite of look down on.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The dog wagged ________ tail when it saw the children.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) its
Why: "Its" (no apostrophe) is the possessive form: the tail belongs to the dog.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) mean "it is". (C) is not an English word.
Key point: It's = it is; its = belonging to it.

questions.sub_topic: The village where my grandmother lives
questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. has no bus service
B. even today
C. where my grandmother lives
D. The village
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) D, C, A, B
Why: "The village (D) where my grandmother lives (C) has no bus service (A) even today (B)." The "where" clause must follow "The village".
Why not the others: (A) and (B) start with a lower-case part. (D) leaves "The village even today" with its verb at the end, after the "where" clause.
Key point: A relative clause follows the noun it describes.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The boy's ________ invention uses rainwater from the roof to flush the school toilets.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ingenious
Why: "Ingenious" means clever, original and inventive.
Why not the others: (A) "Ingenuous" means innocent and trusting. (C) means native to a place. (D) means very poor.
Key point: Ingenious (clever) and ingenuous (innocent) are often confused.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:
A. Editors then check these reports and decide which ones will appear on each page.
B. Reporters gather news during the day and file their reports by evening.
C. Before dawn, the bundles are loaded into vans and sent to newspaper sellers.
D. Late at night, the finished pages are printed and the copies are tied into bundles.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) B, A, D, C
Why: B begins with the reporters; A continues with "these reports" and the editors; D follows ("Late at night ... bundles"); C ends "Before dawn, the bundles".
Why not the others: (A) prints the pages before they are edited. (C) begins with "these reports". (D) loads "the bundles" before they are made.
Key point: Time phrases and "these" link the steps.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
His work this term has been ________, though not excellent.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) satisfactory
Why: After "has been", an adjective is needed; "satisfactory" means good enough.
Why not the others: (A) is a verb. (B) is a noun. (D) is an adverb.
Key point: "Satisfactory" means acceptable; "satisfying" means giving pleasure.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The bridge was damaged in the flood; ________ all traffic has been diverted.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) hence
Why: "Hence" means "for this reason"; the diversion results from the damage.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) show contrast. (B) shows a condition.
Key point: Hence = therefore.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
The heavy rain prevented us ________ going to the fair.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) from
Why: The pattern is "prevent someone from doing something".
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are not used in this pattern.
Key point: Prevent from, stop from, prohibit from.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. remained closed
B. on Monday
C. for the festival
D. Most shops in the market
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) D, A, B, C
Why: The capitalised subject (D) is followed by the verb (A), the time (B) and the reason (C).
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) start with a lower-case part, so the capitalised subject is lost in the middle.
Key point: A capital letter marks the opening part.

questions.question:
Match the figures of speech in List-I with the examples in List-II:

List-I
(A) Hyperbole
(B) Metonymy
(C) Personification
(D) Simile

List-II
(I) Delhi has announced new rules for schools.
(II) The old clock coughed and struck nine.
(III) Her tears flowed like a river in flood.
(IV) I have been waiting for you for a hundred years.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(III)
Why: "A hundred years" exaggerates — hyperbole (IV); "Delhi" stands for the government — metonymy (I); a clock that coughs — personification (II); "like a river in flood" — simile (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps hyperbole and metonymy; (B) swaps metonymy and personification; (C) swaps the last two.
Key point: In metonymy, a related name stands for the thing meant.

questions.question:
Select the words that mean "to make something less severe or painful":
A. alleviate
B. aggravate
C. mitigate
D. elevate
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B and C only
D) A, C and D only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A and C only
Why: "Alleviate" and "mitigate" both mean to make pain or a problem less severe.
Why not the others: B (aggravate) means to make worse — the opposite. D (elevate) means to raise. Options (A), (B) and (D) include one of them.
Key point: Medicines alleviate pain; rash words aggravate quarrels.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
________ some students prefer to study in the morning, others work best at night.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) While
Why: "While" can show contrast between two facts, like "whereas".
Why not the others: (A) gives a reason. (C) gives a condition. (D) gives a purpose.
Key point: While can mean "during" or "whereas"; here it contrasts.

questions.question:
Match the phrasal verbs in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) Pull through
(B) Pull off
(C) Pull out
(D) Pull up

List-II
(I) Recover from a serious illness or difficulty
(II) Succeed in doing something difficult
(III) Withdraw from an agreement or an event
(IV) Bring a vehicle to a stop
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: The patient pulled through — recovered (I); pull off a surprise win — succeed (II); pull out of a deal — withdraw (III); the bus pulled up — stopped (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the first two; (C) swaps the middle two; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: The particle changes the meaning of "pull".

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in the passive voice:
We can solve this problem easily.
options: A) This problem can solved easily.
B) This problem could be solved easily by us.
C) This problem can be solving easily.
D) This problem can be solved easily.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) This problem can be solved easily.
Why: Modal + be + past participle: "can be solved". The agent "we" may be left out.
Why not the others: (A) drops "be". (B) changes "can" to "could". (C) uses "solving".
Key point: Can/may/must + be + past participle.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.sub_topic: Correct sentences: used to, since, physics, discussed
questions.question:
Which of the following sentences are grammatically correct?
A. I am used to getting up early.
B. She has been working here for 2015.
C. Physics is easier than chemistry for me.
D. They discussed about the problem for an hour.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B and C only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A and C only
Why: In A, "be used to" is followed by the -ing form. In C, "physics" takes a singular verb.
Why not the others: B should be "since 2015" (a point in time). D should be "discussed the problem" ("discuss" takes no preposition). Options (A), (B) and (D) include B or D.
Key point: Discuss a topic, not discuss about it.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
This year there were ________ accidents on the highway than last year.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) fewer
Why: "Fewer" is used with countable plural nouns such as "accidents".
Why not the others: (A) "Less" is used with uncountable nouns (less water). (B) means smaller in importance. (C) is the superlative.
Key point: Fewer cars, less traffic.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
More than two hundred schools will ________ part in the science fair.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) take
Why: The fixed collocation is "take part in", meaning to participate.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) do not go with "part" in this sense.
Key point: Take part, take place, take turns.

questions.question: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to DIMINISH:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Increase
Why: Diminish means to become or make smaller; increase means to become or make larger.
Why not the others: (A) is a synonym. (C) and (D) are unrelated.
Key point: Diminishing returns are returns that keep getting smaller.

questions.question:
Match the words in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) Austere
(B) Docile
(C) Haughty
(D) Impetuous

List-II
(I) Arrogantly proud
(II) Acting quickly without thinking
(III) Simple and strict, without comforts
(IV) Quiet and easily controlled
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Austere — strict and plain, as in an austere life (III); docile — gentle and obedient (IV); haughty — proud and looking down on others (I); impetuous — rash and hasty (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps austere and docile; (B) swaps docile and haughty; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: An impetuous decision is made in a hurry.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to ENORMOUS:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Huge
Why: Enormous means very large; huge means the same.
Why not the others: (A) is the opposite. (B) only looks similar. (D) is unrelated.
Key point: An enormous elephant is a huge one.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to complete the sentence that begins: "The teacher was pleased"
A. had finished the project
B. from their parents
C. that the students
D. without any help
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) C, A, D, B
Why: "The teacher was pleased that the students (C) had finished the project (A) without any help (D) from their parents (B)."
Why not the others: (B) separates "the students" from "had finished". (C) and (D) put a phrase before "that the students" and leave the clause broken.
Key point: Subject and verb of a "that" clause stay together.

questions.question: Choose the one word for: "A group of ships sailing together or under one command"
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Fleet
Why: A fleet is a group of ships (or vehicles) under one control.
Why not the others: (A) is used for birds or sheep. (C) is used for cattle. (D) is used for insects.
Key point: Collective nouns depend on what is grouped.

questions.question:
Match the words in List-I with their definitions in List-II:

List-I
(A) Biography
(B) Monologue
(C) Anthology
(D) Manuscript

List-II
(I) A collection of poems or stories by different writers
(II) The story of a person's life written by someone else
(III) A book or document written by hand, or an author's original text
(IV) A long speech by one actor or speaker
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Biography — a life story written by another (II); monologue — a long speech by one person (IV); anthology — a collection by different writers (I); manuscript — a handwritten or original text (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps biography and monologue; (C) swaps monologue and anthology; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: "Mono-" one; "manu-" hand.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in indirect speech:
The old man said, "Honesty is the best policy."
options: A) The old man said that honesty is the best policy.
B) The old man said that honesty was the best policy.
C) The old man told that honesty had been the best policy.
D) The old man said that honesty will be the best policy.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The old man said that honesty is the best policy.
Why: A universal truth or proverb keeps its present tense in reported speech, even after a past reporting verb.
Why not the others: (B) shifts the tense, which is not done for universal truths. (C) uses "told" without an object and the wrong tense. (D) changes to the future.
Key point: Universal truths do not change tense.

questions.question:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in capitals:
The winter in Bengaluru is usually MILD.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Severe
Why: Mild weather is not extreme; severe weather is harsh and extreme.
Why not the others: (A) is close in meaning. (B) and (D) describe winter but are not opposites.
Key point: Mild and severe can describe weather, illness or punishment.

questions.sub_topic: Synonym pairs: vanish, brave, foe, permit
questions.question:
Select the correct pairs of synonyms:
A. vanish — disappear
B. brave — cowardly
C. foe — enemy
D. permit — allow
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, C and D only
C) B, C and D only
D) A, B, C and D
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A, C and D only
Why: Vanish and disappear, foe and enemy, permit and allow have the same meaning.
Why not the others: Pair B is a pair of antonyms. Options (B), (C) and (D) include pair B.
Key point: Test each pair on its own.

questions.question:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in capitals:
The old teacher's speech was full of PROFOUND ideas about life.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Deep
Why: Profound means showing great knowledge or insight; deep has this sense.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) do not mean full of insight.
Key point: A profound thought goes deep below the surface.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
From his silence, we ________ that he did not agree with the plan.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) inferred
Why: To "infer" is to reach a conclusion from evidence; the listeners concluded something from his silence.
Why not the others: (B) To "imply" is to suggest something without saying it; it is the speaker who implies. (C) means mentioned. (D) means postponed.
Key point: The speaker implies; the listener infers.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correctly formed word to fill in the blank:
Her ________ of French words is excellent.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) pronunciation
Why: The noun from "pronounce" (meaning the way a word is said) is "pronunciation", spelt without the "o" after "n".
Why not the others: (A) is a common misspelling. (C) means a formal announcement. (D) is a verb.
Key point: Pronounce, but pronunciation.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correctly spelt word to fill in the blank:
The washing machine comes with a two-year ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) guarantee
Why: The correct spelling is g-u-a-r-a-n-t-e-e.
Why not the others: (A) misses the "u". (B) has "e" in place of the second "a". (D) doubles the "r".
Key point: Guarantee has a silent "u" after "g".

questions.sub_topic: Idioms: two birds one stone, square one, spilt milk, long run
questions.question:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) To kill two birds with one stone
(B) Back to square one
(C) To cry over spilt milk
(D) In the long run

List-II
(I) Back to the beginning, after a failure
(II) Over a long period of time; eventually
(III) To achieve two aims with one action
(IV) To be upset about something that cannot be changed
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Kill two birds with one stone — two aims, one action (III); back to square one — start again (I); cry over spilt milk — regret what cannot be undone (IV); in the long run — eventually (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two; (B) swaps the middle two; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: Learn idioms as whole units of meaning.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to EPITOME:
options: C) Summary of a book only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Perfect example
Why: An epitome is a perfect example of a quality or type: she is the epitome of kindness.
Why not the others: (A) is the closing part of a book and only looks similar. (B) is unrelated. (C) is an older, narrow sense and does not fit "a perfect example of".
Key point: The epitome of courage is courage in its purest form.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. when the phone rang
B. Hardly had she
C. to her dinner
D. sat down
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) B, D, C, A
Why: "Hardly had she (B) sat down (D) to her dinner (C) when the phone rang (A)."
Why not the others: (A) puts "when" before the participle. (C) starts with a lower-case part. (D) puts "to her dinner" before "sat down".
Key point: Hardly had + subject + past participle ... when.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
The new scheme aims ________ providing clean drinking water to every village.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) at
Why: "Aim at" is used before a noun or an -ing form: aims at providing.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are not standard here. (C) "Aim to" is followed by a base verb ("aims to provide"), not an -ing form.
Key point: Aim at + -ing; aim to + verb.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Copying the same sentence a hundred times was a ________ punishment.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) tedious
Why: "Tedious" means long, slow and boring.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) contradict copying the same sentence a hundred times.
Key point: The situation tells you the word.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Before the printing press, every book had to be copied by hand. A single copy could take months, so books were rare and costly, and most people never owned one. In the middle of the fifteenth century, Johannes Gutenberg of Mainz in Germany developed a press that used movable metal type: small blocks, each carrying one letter, which could be arranged into pages, inked, printed and then used again. Hundreds of copies of the same page could now be produced in the time it once took to write a few.

Printing reached India in 1556, when Portuguese missionaries set up a press in Goa. For more than two centuries, however, it was used mainly for religious texts. India's first newspaper did not appear until 1780, when an Irishman, James Augustus Hicky, began publishing Hicky's Bengal Gazette in Calcutta. It was full of gossip and sharp attacks on officials of the East India Company. The Company was not amused: by 1782 Hicky's press had been seized and the paper closed.

Indian reformers soon saw that the press could be a voice for their own ideas. In the 1820s, Raja Ram Mohan Roy started journals in Bengali and Persian that discussed social reform and public questions. By the end of the nineteenth century, newspapers in English and in many Indian languages were spreading news and nationalist ideas to readers far beyond the big cities. The British government grew so worried about the Indian-language press that in 1878 it passed the Vernacular Press Act to control it.

The story of printing in India is therefore not only about machines. It is about who has the right to speak, and who gets to listen.

Question: According to the passage, what was special about Gutenberg's press?
options: A) It printed only religious books
B) It was operated by Portuguese missionaries
C) It copied books by hand much faster than before
D) It used movable metal type that could be reused
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) It used movable metal type that could be reused
Why: Gutenberg "developed a press that used movable metal type: small blocks, each carrying one letter, which could be arranged into pages, inked, printed and then used again."
Why not the others: (A) The religious use refers to printing in Goa. (B) The missionaries came later, in India. (C) Printing replaced copying by hand.
Key point: Match each detail to the right place in the passage.

Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: Why was Hicky's Bengal Gazette closed in 1782?
options: A) It ran out of money to buy paper
B) It attacked East India Company officials
D) Indian reformers objected to its gossip
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) It attacked East India Company officials
Why: The paper was "full of gossip and sharp attacks on officials of the East India Company. The Company was not amused: by 1782 Hicky's press had been seized."
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not stated.
Key point: A colon often introduces a result.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Before the printing press, every book had to be copied by hand. A single copy could take months, so books were rare and costly, and most people never owned one. In the middle of the fifteenth century, Johannes Gutenberg of Mainz in Germany developed a press that used movable metal type: small blocks, each carrying one letter, which could be arranged into pages, inked, printed and then used again. Hundreds of copies of the same page could now be produced in the time it once took to write a few.

It was full of gossip and sharp attacks on officials of the East India Company. The Company was not amused: by 1782 Hicky's press had been seized and the paper closed.

Indian reformers soon saw that the press could be a voice for their own ideas. In the 1820s, Raja Ram Mohan Roy started journals in Bengali and Persian that discussed social reform and public questions. The British government grew so worried about the Indian-language press that in 1878 it passed the Vernacular Press Act to control it.

The story of printing in India is therefore not only about machines. It is about who has the right to speak, and who gets to listen.

Question: "The Company was not amused." This is a polite way of saying that the Company:
options: B) Did not find the paper funny
C) Had not read the newspaper
D) Was too busy to notice
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Was angry and displeased
Why: The understatement is explained by what follows: the press was seized and the paper closed, actions of an angry authority.
Why not the others: (B) reads the phrase literally. (C) and (D) contradict the seizure.
Key point: Understatement says less than is meant; the consequences show the real meaning.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Before the printing press, every book had to be copied by hand. A single copy could take months, so books were rare and costly, and most people never owned one. In the middle of the fifteenth century, Johannes Gutenberg of Mainz in Germany developed a press that used movable metal type: small blocks, each carrying one letter, which could be arranged into pages, inked, printed and then used again. Question: What can be inferred about why the British passed the Vernacular Press Act in 1878?
options: A) They wanted to help Indian-language newspapers grow
B) They wished to replace English newspapers with Indian ones
C) They feared that Indian-language papers were spreading nationalist ideas
D) They wanted to stop missionaries from printing religious books
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) They feared that Indian-language papers were spreading nationalist ideas
Why: The passage links the spread of "news and nationalist ideas" by Indian-language papers to the government being "so worried" that it passed the Act "to control it".
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are the opposite. (D) is unrelated to the Act.
Key point: An inference joins two stated facts.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Before the printing press, every book had to be copied by hand. A single copy could take months, so books were rare and costly, and most people never owned one. In the middle of the fifteenth century, Johannes Gutenberg of Mainz in Germany developed a press that used movable metal type: small blocks, each carrying one letter, which could be arranged into pages, inked, printed and then used again. Hundreds of copies of the same page could now be produced in the time it once took to write a few.

Printing reached India in 1556, when Portuguese missionaries set up a press in Goa. For more than two centuries, however, it was used mainly for religious texts. India's first newspaper did not appear until 1780, when an Irishman, James Augustus Hicky, began publishing Hicky's Bengal Gazette in Calcutta. It was full of gossip and sharp attacks on officials of the East India Company. The Company was not amused: by 1782 Hicky's press had been seized and the paper closed.

Indian reformers soon saw that the press could be a voice for their own ideas. In the 1820s, Raja Ram Mohan Roy started journals in Bengali and Persian that discussed social reform and public questions. By the end of the nineteenth century, newspapers in English and in many Indian languages were spreading news and nationalist ideas to readers far beyond the big cities. The British government grew so worried about the Indian-language press that in 1878 it passed the Vernacular Press Act to control it.

The story of printing in India is therefore not only about machines. It is about who has the right to speak, and who gets to listen.

Question: What is the writer's main point in the last paragraph?
options: A) Printing machines in India were of poor quality
B) Newspapers were less important than religious books
C) Printing came to India too late to be useful
D) Printing in India was linked to the power to speak and be heard
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Printing in India was linked to the power to speak and be heard
Why: The writer concludes that the story "is about who has the right to speak, and who gets to listen."
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not stated or suggested.
Key point: The final paragraph often gives the writer's view of the whole.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Ananya had not lost a game of chess in two years. She had beaten every child in her school, three teachers and, once, the uncle who had taught her the moves. So when she arrived at her first state-level tournament, eleven years old and wearing her lucky blue hairband, she was quietly sure she would win.

Her first-round opponent was a tall, silent boy of fourteen who wrote down every move in a small notebook. For twenty moves the game was even. Then Ananya saw a chance to win his bishop. She took it at once, with a little flick of her fingers, and looked up to see whether he had noticed.

He had. Three moves later, his knight landed on a square she had not even looked at, and she realised, with a cold feeling in her stomach, that the bishop had been bait. Her queen was trapped. She played on for another ten moves, hoping for a miracle, and then laid her king down on its side.

She did not cry until she reached the corridor. Her coach found her there and sat beside her on the bench without saying anything for a long time.

"Show me," he said at last, and handed her a pocket set. She set up the position. "Here," he said, touching the bishop. "Why did you take it?"

"Because it was free."

"Nothing on a chessboard is free," he said. "Ask what it costs."

That night, in a new notebook, Ananya wrote down every move of the game. At the top of the first page she wrote: "Lesson one." She won her next four games.

Question: Before the tournament, Ananya had:
options: A) Not lost a game of chess in two years
B) Lost to her uncle in every game
C) Played in many state-level tournaments
D) Never played against a teacher
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Not lost a game of chess in two years
Why: "Ananya had not lost a game of chess in two years." It was "her first state-level tournament".
Why not the others: (B) She had once beaten her uncle. (C) It was her first. (D) She had beaten three teachers.
Key point: Detail questions are answered from the exact lines.

Question: "The bishop had been bait." This means that the bishop:
options: A) Had been placed there by mistake
B) Had been offered on purpose to trap her
C) Was the most valuable piece on the board
D) Was protected by her own knight
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Had been offered on purpose to trap her
Why: Bait is something offered to attract and trap. By taking it, she let his knight trap her queen.

Question: What does the coach mean by "Nothing on a chessboard is free. Ask what it costs"?
options: A) Chess sets should not be given away
B) She should not play in tournaments that charge fees
C) She should always take pieces as quickly as possible
D) Before taking an offered gain, she should look for its hidden price
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Before taking an offered gain, she should look for its hidden price
Why: The "free" bishop cost her the queen. The coach teaches her to think about what an apparent gift may lead to.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) take "free" literally. (C) is the mistake she made.
Key point: Advice in a story often applies beyond its setting.

questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) She has decided to learn from defeat
Why: She records the game to study it, as her opponent did, and her improved results ("She won her next four games") show she has learnt.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

For two months the earth had been waiting. The fields had cracked into a pattern of dry tiles, the pond had shrunk to a cake of mud where the buffaloes stood in hopeless patience, and the leaves of the mango trees hung grey with dust. Every afternoon clouds gathered over the hills, looked down at the thirsty land and drifted away again, like rich relatives who promise and never come.

Then, one evening, the wind changed. It came from the south, damp and sudden, and the tops of the trees began to toss. The light turned a strange yellow-green. Somewhere a door banged, and the hens ran for cover with their wings half open.

The first drops were enormous. They fell far apart, each one striking the dust with a small soft explosion, and where they struck, the earth darkened in coins. Then the whole sky opened, and the rain came down in grey ropes, drumming on the tin sheds, hissing on the hot stones, filling the cracks in the fields as if it were trying to stitch the land together again.

And the smell — that is what everyone remembers. It rose from the soaked ground all at once, rich and earthy and green, the smell of every childhood monsoon. Children ran out to dance in the courtyards. Old men stood in their doorways with their palms held out, catching the water as if it were a gift, which of course it was.

Question: "Clouds ... drifted away again, like rich relatives who promise and never come." This simile suggests that the clouds:
options: A) Raised hopes of rain but disappointed them
B) Brought gifts to the village
C) Were very large and dark
D) Were visiting the hills for a festival
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Raised hopes of rain but disappointed them
Why: Like relatives who promise visits and never arrive, the clouds gathered every afternoon but did not bring rain.
Why not the others: (C) is not the point of the comparison. (B) and (D) take it literally.
Key point: Ask what the two things compared have in common.

Question: "Where they struck, the earth darkened in coins." This image means that:
options: A) Coins had been buried in the dry fields
B) Each raindrop left a small round dark spot
C) The rain washed away the villagers' money
D) The earth turned the colour of copper coins
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Each raindrop left a small round dark spot
Why: The large, separate first drops made round, coin-sized wet marks on the dusty ground.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) take the image literally. (D) The earth "darkened"; it did not turn copper.
Key point: Picture the image to understand it.

Question: The rain fills the cracks "as if it were trying to stitch the land together again". The figure of speech here is chiefly:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Personification
Why: The rain is imagined as deliberately trying to sew up the cracked land, a human action — personification.
Why not the others: (A) No opposites are joined. (B) No sounds are repeated at the start of words. (C) It is an imaginative picture, not an exaggeration.
Key point: "As if it were trying to ..." gives intention to something non-human.

Question: The old men catch the water "as if it were a gift, which of course it was". What does the writer suggest?
options: A) The rain was sent by the government as relief
B) The old men were greedy for water
C) After the long drought, the rain truly was a blessing
D) The old men did not understand what rain was
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) After the long drought, the rain truly was a blessing
Why: The writer agrees with the old men: after months of cracked fields and dried ponds, the rain really was a precious gift.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not suggested.
Key point: "Of course" shows the writer's own view.
